extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and instructors of a one-semester basic real analysis course (e.g., Math 444/521), and self-learners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for using/teaching from this Basic Analysis I textbook: prerequisites, recommended section-by-section syllabus for different paces, pedagogical and notational conventions, licensing, and topic ordering for a one-semester (or year-long with Volume II) course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing terms
rubrics_metrics.description: This work is dual licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License and the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International License.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can use, print, duplicate, and share this book as much as you want. You can base your own notes on it and reuse parts if you keep the license the same. You can assume the license is either CC-BY-NC-SA or CC-BY-SA, whichever is compatible with what you wish to do. Your derivative work must use at least one of the licenses. Derivative works must be prominently marked as such. (Links to the license URLs are provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended course scope (one-semester vs year-long)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This first volume is a one semester course in basic analysis. With the second volume, it is a year-long course."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Volume I alone for a one-semester course; use Volume I + II for a year-long course that covers multivariable topics. For a year-long plan, cover most of Volume I in the first semester and leave metric spaces for the start of the second semester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A prerequisite for these courses is usually a basic proof course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests prior exposure to a basic proofs text (examples cited: Hammack [H], Fields [F], or D'Angelo & West [DW]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested section-by-section selections for different paces
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete lists of sections to cover for a slower (UIUC 444) and a more rigorous (UW 521) one-semester course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slower course (UIUC 444) suggestion: §0.3, §1.1–§1.4, §2.1–§2.5, §3.1–§3.4, §4.1–§4.2, §5.1–§5.3, §6.1–§6.3. More rigorous course covering metric spaces (UW 521): §0.3, §1.1–§1.4, §2.1–§2.5, §3.1–§3.4, §4.1–§4.2, §5.1–§5.3, §6.1–§6.2, §7.1–§7.6. The author also notes it is possible to run a faster course without metric spaces covering all sections of chapters 0 through 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture pacing / estimated lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: The approximate number of lectures given in the section notes through Chapter 6 are a very rough estimate and were designed for the slower course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections include notes like "Note: 1–3 lectures" for §0.3 and other per-section rough lecture counts; instructors may skip, cover lightly, or leave material as reading depending on course speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to the Riemann integral
rubrics_metrics.description: "A major difference is that we define the Riemann integral using Darboux sums and not tagged partitions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's rationale: "The Darboux approach is far more appropriate for a course of this level." Instructors who follow this book are expected to teach the Darboux (upper/lower sum) approach rather than the tagged-partition (Riemann sum) approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof style and pedagogical conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Author preference and guidance on proof methods and formality: prefer direct proofs/contrapositive over contradiction when possible; avoid unnecessary formalism; proofs and language become slightly less formal as the book progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact wording: "Many proofs traditionally done by contradiction, I prefer to do by a direct proof or by contrapositive. While the book does include proofs by contradiction, I only do so when the contrapositive statement seemed too awkward or when contradiction follows rather quickly. Contradiction is more likely to get beginning students into trouble... I try to avoid unnecessary formalism where it is unhelpful. Furthermore, the proofs and the language get slightly less formal as we progress through the book, as more and more details are left out to avoid clutter." This serves as a stylistic rubric for writing/teaching proofs in this course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational conventions (definition symbol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ':=' instead of '=' to define an object rather than to simply show equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses the ':=' symbol liberally, even for local definitions (example paraphrase: using ':=' even for defining x^2 in a single exercise). Instructors/authors adapting the text should follow this convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course topic ordering & learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The book orders topics to build foundations: real numbers (completeness), sequences and limits, functions of one variable (continuity, derivative), the Riemann integral, sequences of functions and interchange of limits, and an introduction to metric spaces culminating in Picard's theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated learning goals: acquaint the reader with rigorous proofs in analysis and set a firm foundation for single-variable calculus (and several variables with Volume II). The pedagogical arc emphasizes completeness of the reals as central, then sequences, then functions and integrals, finishing with metric spaces and fixed-point/Picard applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to different student populations
rubrics_metrics.description: The book "should be possible to use ... for both a basic course for students who do not necessarily wish to go to graduate school ... and also as a more advanced one-semester course that also covers topics such as metric spaces."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author indicates adaptability: the same material can be paced and selected for less advanced students (e.g., UIUC 444) or more advanced ones (e.g., UW 521), and earlier chapters can be used in an introductory proofs course (e.g., Math 201 paired with Hammack).
